message:
QUESTION:
Under company policy, which of the five stores should receive this year's refurbishment budget?

DATA:
Five-store retail chain, financial year 2025. A refurbishment budget is available for one store. Company policy: the budget goes to the store with the lowest annual sales per square foot of sales floor (the company's space-productivity KPI), measured on a full-year basis.

| Store | Annual sales 2025 | Sales floor area (sq ft) | Gross internal area incl. stockrooms (sq ft) |
| North | £2.4m | 8,000 | 10,000 |
| South | £3.6m | 15,000 | 18,000 |
| East | £1.8m | 6,000 | 9,000 |
| West | £2.1m | 10,000 | 12,000 |
| Central | £4.2m | 12,000 | 14,000 |

Annual sales 2024: North £2.3m, South £3.5m, East £1.7m, West £2.9m, Central £4.0m. Floor areas were the same in 2024.

Operations note: West was closed from January to March 2025 (3 months) for flood repairs, so its 2025 sales cover 9 trading months. All other stores traded for all 12 months in both years. The flood repairs were covered by insurance and did not change the store's layout.

Here is your current analysis:

<analysis>
# Critical Review

I rechecked every figure against the source data. The KPIs, chain averages (£290 and £282), gross-area figures, the £2.4m break-even and the 12.5% threshold are all correct. **South is the right answer.** The remaining problems are in the reasoning:

| # | Issue | Why it matters | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The "−3%" underlying change is stated as fact, but it is a product of the method.** It relies on straight 12/9 pro-rating. Section 3 then says this method probably *overstates* West. If Q1 is 20% of the year, West's full year is £2.1m ÷ 0.8 = £2.625m, which is −9% on 2024. | Section 2 uses the fact that West "held its level" to support its case, while Section 3 undermines it. Section 4 repeats the claim ("close to its own 2024 level"). | Give a range (−3% to about −9%). Rest the case on the break-even, which holds anywhere in that range. |
| 2 | **The history cross-check works against its own premise.** "If 2025 matched 2024, Q1 = £0.8m" implies Q1 was 28% of the year, above an average quarter. The analysis has just argued Q1 is usually *below* average. | The check proves less than it appears to and conflicts with the seasonality argument. | Replace it with a cleaner test. West falls below South only if its full year is under £2.4m. That would be a 17% fall on 2024, while every other store grew 3–6%. |
| 3 | **An unsourced benchmark is presented as fact.** The claim "a weak Q1 typically makes up about 20% of the year" comes from no data in the brief. | The robustness argument appears to rest on outside evidence that is not given. | Present 20% as an illustrative assumption. The argument does not need it, because the threshold is 12.5%, half an even quarter. |
| 4 | **The review section undercuts the deliverable.** It lists "audit history in the deliverable" as a flaw, yet opens the document with a review table. | A decision-maker gets process commentary first. | Keep the review separate from the deliverable, as here. |
| 5 | **Minor overreach.** Calling the actual-sales reading "the weakest of the four" is opinion. The gross-area aside adds little to a decision made on sales floor. | Small hits to credibility. | Soften the first point. Reduce the gross-area point to one line. |

---

# Refurbishment Budget Allocation, FY2025

## Recommendation

**Under company policy, the refurbishment budget should go to South.** On a full-year basis, South had the lowest sales per square foot of sales floor in 2025 (£240). It was also lowest in 2024 (£233).

West's headline figure (£210) is lower. However, it reflects only 9 trading months because of an insured flood closure. Policy requires a full-year basis. Annualised, West is £280: second-lowest, and £40 above South.

## 1. KPI: annual sales ÷ sales floor area

West annualised: £2.1m × 12/9 = £2.8m. Its floor area is unchanged, because the repairs did not alter the layout.

| Store | 2025 sales (full-year basis) | Sales floor (sq ft) | 2025 £/sq ft | 2024 £/sq ft | Sales change 2024→25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| North | £2.4m | 8,000 | £300 | £288 | +4% |
| **South** | **£3.6m** | **15,000** | **£240** | **£233** | +3% |
| East | £1.8m | 6,000 | £300 | £283 | +6% |
| West | £2.8m (£2.1m actual, 9 months) | 10,000 | £280 (£210 unadjusted) | £290 | −3% to −9%* |
| Central | £4.2m | 12,000 | £350 | £333 | +5% |
| **Chain** | **£14.8m** (£14.1m reported) | **51,000** | **£290** | **£282** | |

\*The range depends on the seasonal weight of the missing quarter. It is −3% with straight pro-rating and about −9% if Q1 is 20% of annual sales.

**2025 ranking, lowest first:** South £240, West £280, North and East £300 each, Central £350. South is about 17% below the chain average in both years.

On gross internal area, which is not the policy measure, South is still tied-lowest (£200, with East).

## 2. Why West's headline figure does not decide the matter

- West's £2.1m covers 9 months. Every other store's figure covers 12. Comparing them directly understates West by a quarter.
- The closure was a one-off: insured, and with no change to layout. It says nothing about West's space productivity, which is what the KPI measures.

## 3. Robustness

**Break-even.** West ranks below South only if its true full-year sales were under £2.4m. That would mean its missing Q1 was worth less than £0.3m, or 12.5% of the year. Two checks make this implausible:

- **Seasonality.** An even quarter is 25% of the year. A Q1 at 12.5% would be half a normal quarter. That is far weaker than ordinary seasonal patterns, even though January to March is typically soft and West's 9 months include Christmas.
- **History.** A full year under £2.4m would be a 17% fall on West's 2024 sales of £2.9m. Over the same period, every other store grew 3–6%. Nothing in the data suggests a decline of that size at West.

Straight pro-rating probably flatters West slightly, so its true figure may be nearer £260 than £280. That is still clearly above South. Weak trading just after reopening would push the other way, making the 9-month figure understate West's normal run-rate.

**Interpretations of "full-year basis":**

| Reading | Result |
|---|---|
| Annualise part-year stores (used above) | South |
| Only stores with 12 trading months are eligible | South (West excluded) |
| Use the latest full year for a part-year store (West 2024: £290) | South |
| Use actual sales in the year, closure included (West £210) | West |

Only the last reading favours West, and it fits the policy wording poorly. The policy already says *annual* sales. The phrase "measured on a full-year basis" adds something only if it means adjusting for part-year trading. That reading would also direct the budget according to a flood, not space productivity. Because the wording permits it, the policy should still be clarified (Section 5).

**Persistence.** South was the lowest-density store in both years. Its position is structural, not a one-year dip.

## 4. Decision

**Allocate the refurbishment budget to South.**

Do not prioritise West. Under any reasonable seasonal assumption, its full-year density is £260–280, well clear of South's £240.

## 5. Follow-up

- **Clarify the policy.** State how part-year stores are treated, for example annualised using seasonal weights.
- **Use monthly data if it exists.** It would let West's Q1 be estimated from its own seasonal pattern instead of by pro-rating.
- **Check the scope of the works.** South has the chain's largest sales floor (15,000 sq ft). Its low density may partly reflect excess space, not the store's condition. The plan should consider reallocating space, not just cosmetic works.
- **Plan the timing.** Schedule works outside peak trading. If South closes during them, report its KPI on a full-year basis, as done here for West.
- **Measure the effect.** Compare South's sales density over the 12 full trading months after the works with the rest of the chain over the same period.
</analysis>

Review it critically and produce an improved version.
response:
# Review of the current analysis

I rechecked every figure against the brief. All the KPIs, the chain averages, the gross-area figures, the £2.4m break-even, the 12.5% threshold and the 17% gaps are arithmetically correct. **South remains the right answer.** The remaining problems are presentation and precision:

| # | Issue | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The rounding is slightly off.** £2.1m ÷ 0.8 = £2.625m, which is −9.5% on £2.9m. "About −9%" understates it, and "−3%" is really −3.4%. | Give the range as roughly −3% to −10%. |
| 2 | **One connective is wrong.** "Far weaker than ordinary seasonal patterns, *even though* January to March is typically soft" reads as a contradiction. The soft-Q1 point is a concession, not a contrast. | Use "even allowing for a soft Q1". Mark the soft-Q1 claim as general retail experience, not data from the brief. |
| 3 | **The interpretation argument overstates its case.** The claim that "full-year basis" only adds meaning if it means adjusting is not airtight. The phrase could just be emphasis, ruling out monthly or peak-period figures. | Rest the case on the KPI's stated purpose (space productivity). A flood closure says nothing about that. Admit that the literal wording is ambiguous. |
| 4 | **"Structural" is too strong.** Two years of data is thin evidence. | Say "consistent across both years". |
| 5 | **A possible West decline is not stated plainly.** With seasonal weighting, West's April–December trading fell by up to about 10%. That is worth monitoring, even though it doesn't change the ranking. | Add one line to the follow-ups. |
| 6 | **The document still mixes the review with the deliverable and repeats itself.** The Decision section restates the Recommendation, and the review table sits above the deliverable. | Keep the review above the divider and remove the duplicate Decision section. |

---

# Refurbishment Budget Allocation, FY2025

## Recommendation

**The refurbishment budget should go to South.** On a full-year basis it had the chain's lowest sales per square foot of sales floor in 2025 (£240). It was also lowest in 2024 (£233).

West's unadjusted figure (£210) is lower. However, it covers only 9 trading months because of an insured flood closure. On a full-year basis West is about £280, which is second-lowest and £40 above South.

## 1. KPI: annual sales ÷ sales floor area

West's full-year estimate is £2.1m × 12/9 = £2.8m. Its floor area is unchanged, because the repairs did not alter the layout.

| Store | 2025 sales (full-year basis) | Sales floor (sq ft) | 2025 £/sq ft | 2024 £/sq ft | Sales change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| North | £2.4m | 8,000 | £300 | £288 | +4% |
| **South** | **£3.6m** | **15,000** | **£240** | **£233** | +3% |
| East | £1.8m | 6,000 | £300 | £283 | +6% |
| West | £2.8m (actual £2.1m, 9 months) | 10,000 | £280 (unadjusted £210) | £290 | −3% to −10%* |
| Central | £4.2m | 12,000 | £350 | £333 | +5% |
| **Chain** | **£14.8m** (reported £14.1m) | **51,000** | **£290** | **£282** | +3% |

\*The range depends on how much of the year the missing quarter normally represents. It is −3% with straight pro-rating, and about −10% if January–March is 20% of annual sales.

**Ranking for 2025, lowest first:** South £240, West £280, North and East £300 each, Central £350. South is about 17% below the chain average in both years.

## 2. Why West's unadjusted figure does not decide it

- West's £2.1m covers 9 months, while every other store's figure covers 12. A direct comparison understates West by roughly a quarter.
- The KPI measures space productivity. The closure was a one-off: it was insured and did not change the layout. It tells us nothing about how productively West uses its space.

## 3. Robustness

**Break-even.** West would rank below South only if its true full-year sales were under £2.4m. That would mean the missing January–March quarter was worth less than £0.3m, or 12.5% of the year. That is half an average quarter. The figure is implausible on two counts:

- **Seasonality.** Even allowing for January–March being a soft quarter in most retail (general experience, not data in the brief), a quarter worth half the average is extreme.
- **History.** A full year under £2.4m would be a 17% fall on West's 2024 sales of £2.9m, while every other store grew 3–6%.

Straight pro-rating probably flatters West a little, because its 9 trading months include Christmas. A more realistic seasonal weighting puts West nearer £260, which is still clearly above South. Weak trading just after reopening would push the other way.

**How "full-year basis" is read:**

| Reading | Budget goes to |
|---|---|
| Annualise part-year stores (used above) | South |
| Only stores that traded all 12 months are eligible | South |
| Use the latest full year for a part-year store (West 2024: £290) | South |
| Use actual sales in the year, closure included (West £210) | West |

Only the last reading favours West. The literal wording does not rule it out. However, that reading would allocate the budget because of a flood, not because of weak space productivity, which defeats the purpose of the KPI.

**Consistency.** South was the lowest-density store in both years available, so this is not a one-year dip.

## 4. Follow-up

- **Clarify the policy** so it states how part-year stores are treated, for example annualised using seasonal weights. The policy owner should confirm the reading used here.
- **Use monthly sales data if it exists.** It would let West's missing quarter be estimated from its own seasonal pattern instead of by pro-rating.
- **Watch West.** With seasonal weighting, its sales may have fallen by up to about 10% while the rest of the chain grew. This doesn't change the allocation, but it should be monitored in 2026.
- **Check the scope of South's works.** South has the largest sales floor (15,000 sq ft). Its low density may partly reflect surplus space rather than the store's condition, so the plan should consider reallocating space as well as cosmetic works.
- **Schedule and measure.** Carry out the works outside peak trading. If South closes during them, report its KPI on a full-year basis, as was done for West here. Then compare South's density over the 12 full trading months after the works with the rest of the chain over the same period.
